questions.prompt: Assuming 64-bit pointers (8 bytes) and std::size_t (8 bytes), what are the sizes of std::span<int, 4> and std::span<int>?
options: a is 8 bytes (pointer only) and b is 16 bytes (pointer plus count)
Both are 16 bytes because every span stores pointer and count
a is 16 bytes (4 ints inline) and b is 16 bytes
a is 24 bytes and b is 16 bytes
questions.explanation: A static-extent std::span<int, 4> encodes the length 4 in its type, so it only needs to store a single T* pointer (8 bytes). A dynamic-extent std::span<int> stores both T* and std::size_t (16 bytes).

questions.prompt: What does the const qualifier on the parameter const std::span<int> s enforce inside the function?
options: Compilation fails because s is const and cannot modify elements
s[0] returns a prvalue copy, leaving the caller's array unchanged
Compilation succeeds and s[0] modifies the caller's underlying int
Compilation fails unless s is passed by const reference
questions.explanation: const on std::span<int> is shallow: it prevents reassigning s itself inside tweak, not mutating the elements it refers to. Read-only element access requires std::span<const int>.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in passing sv.data() to std::puts after slicing with remove_suffix?
options: remove_suffix reallocates the underlying buffer without a terminator
sv.data() still points to the full original string (or non-null-terminated memory), so std::puts prints past the slice or causes undefined behavior
std::string_view::data() returns nullptr after remove_suffix
remove_suffix throws std::out_of_range if sv is shorter than 4 characters
questions.explanation: std::string_view::remove_suffix only decrements the internal length without copying bytes or writing a null terminator. Thus sv.data() still points at the unsliced buffer—printing the removed suffix too or overrunning if the original view was not null-terminated.

questions.prompt: What happens to sv after moving a short SSO std::string a into b?
options: sv automatically updates to point into b's buffer
sv still safely observes "hello" inside b because move steals a heap pointer
std::string_view pins a's buffer via reference counting until sv is destroyed
Moving a short SSO string copies inline bytes and invalidates pointers, references, and views into a; sv no longer refers to b and reading it is invalid
questions.explanation: Under [string.require], moving a std::basic_string invalidates pointers, references, and iterators into the moved-from string. For short strings using SSO, the characters reside directly inside a's footprint and must be copied into b, leaving sv disconnected from b.

questions.prompt: How does C++23 treat the initialization std::string_view sv = nullptr; compared to C++17?
options: In C++17 it selects the const char* constructor causing UB; in C++23 it is ill-formed because the nullptr_t constructor is explicitly deleted
In both C++17 and C++23 it constructs an empty string_view with size 0
In C++23 it throws std::logic_error at runtime
In both C++17 and C++23 it is ill-formed due to ambiguous overloads
questions.explanation: In C++17/C++20, nullptr converted to const char* and invoked basic_string_view(const CharT*), calling Traits::length(nullptr) (UB). C++23 (P2166R1) added basic_string_view(std::nullptr_t) = delete; in [string.view.cons] so it is diagnosed at compile time.

questions.prompt: Given std::string s = "abc";, what does evaluating s[s.size()] produce in C++11 and later?
options: Undefined behavior because s.size() is out of bounds
Throws std::out_of_range
Well-defined: returns a reference to CharT() ('\0'), though writing a non-null value through a non-const reference to s[s.size()] is undefined behavior
Well-defined only when s is const-qualified
questions.explanation: Since C++11, [string.access] guarantees that both const and non-const operator[](size()) return a reference to CharT() (the null terminator). Reading s[s.size()] is well-defined, while modifying it to any value other than CharT() is undefined behavior.
